Unstoppable wallet is purposely built as a decentralized management tool for cryptocurrencies.

It is engineered to serve privacy-conscious individuals looking to manage and invest in Bitcoin, Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies in a sovereign and professional manner.

Unstoppable is built with the following in mind:

- Capital Should Be Free >> It’s built to provide users with genuinely independent control over their capital.

- Capital Should Be Borderless >> It works outside the traditional finance layer and acts as a Swiss knife to the world of decentralized finances (DeFi).

- Capital Should Be Private >> It doesn’t leak private data, it has no means to track users, and takes extra measures to ensure privacy on multiple layers.

If the above rhymes well with you then Unstoppable is for you! And we are here to focus on your unique needs and serve you in the best possible manner.

WALLET FEATURES:

- Non-Custodial Multi-wallet >> Manage any number of cryptocurrencies across multiple portfolio-style wallets in a non-custodial manner. This wallet is like your own bank where you are the only client and the only one in charge. It’s designed to keep assets secure and easy to restore even if the phone is stolen and tampered with.

- Investment Oriented Wallet >> Unstoppable brings unmatched cryptocurrency market analytics to your device: advanced sorting, curated categorization, extensive search filtering, and event-based alerting features.

- Universal Wallet >> It supports all mainstream blockchains and is built in a standard compliant manner enabling users to use just one wallet app for everything crypto.

- A Bitcoin Wallet >> The wallet packs some of the most advanced Bitcoin features available: SPV enabled, BIP 44/49/84/86/69 compliant, Bitcoin timelocks, custom transaction fees, and more.

- A DeFi Wallet >> Full support for decentralized token swaps on Ethereum, Binance Smart Chain, Polygon, Avalanche, Solana, and more. Also, the ability to interact with any smart contract-powered service on the blockchain via the WalletConnect protocol.

- Ethereum Wallet >> Full support for Ethereum blockchain, its growing ecosystem of tokens (ERC20, NFT tokens, etc.), and other decentralized services such as ENS (Ethereum Name Service).

- Ethereum L2 Wallet >> Arbitrum, Optimism, Polygon support.

- Avalanche Wallet >> Full support for Avalanche C-Chain blockchain.

- Binance Wallet >> Full support for original Binance Chain (incl. BEP2) and Binance Smart Chain.

- Crypto Academy >> The app includes two courses meant to onboard newcomers into the world of cryptocurrencies and the DeFi ecosystem in an easy-to-digest manner covering essential aspects of cryptocurrency security, storage, privacy, transacting, and exchanging.

- Wallet for Privacy Coins >> Fully supports major privacy coins (ZCash, DASH) in an SPV manner. One of the very few wallets capable of supporting fully shielded Zcash transactions as well as the ability to privatize Bitcoin transactions.

- Decentralized Wallet >> Designed to work with most major blockchains in a decentralized manner where an app doesn't depend on some server of a wallet provider to send/receive transactions but interacts with blockchain networks directly.

- Privacy Focused >> Designed to allow for privacy even in the most privacy-breaching scenarios. There are no user accounts keeping your records, no identity checks that risk exposing your financials to the world, and no interaction with traditional finance layers. The app is partially TOR enabled and VPN support coming soon.

- Fully Open Source >> The most transparent wallet application built to date. The entire 4-year production process of the app is openly accessible online along with 100% of its code for anyone to evaluate or reuse in other projects. Verified and audited by third parties.

Be Unstoppable!

BitBox02 Nova firmware v9.27.1 (multi) builds reproducibly from source. The official signed

(`cd8b8b64...`) is identical to BitBox02's own v9.27.1 (multi) build, confirming both devices
run the same firmware image, distinguished only by their signature/product ID.

own community-verification period (the release notes explicitly ask for independent
signatures confirming the build), not a beta/test-only build — it ships full release notes,

The official signed firmware binary is downloaded from the tagged GitHub release. Its
first 588 bytes (a 4-byte magic value plus 584 bytes of signature data — 3 root keys and

resigned per-unit and isn't reproducible. The matching tagged commit is cloned from the
public GitHub repository (with submodules) and built inside the project's own Dockerfile
in a containerized `linux/amd64` environment. The stripped official binary is then
compared byte-for-byte against the freshly built (unsigned) binary. A verdict of
`reproducible` requires an exact match.

{"description":"ARM64-v8a APK from GitHub release (split-per-ABI, not universal)","content":"Disclosure: this verification was performed by the wallet's publisher, not an independent third party. It is published so others can repeat it; an independent confirmation would carry more weight.

Result: the rebuilt APK is byte-for-byte identical to the published release asset. Same SHA-256 (2d4edbaad34a157f099333357872a6619b2c03889f87708a679301bae106697d), 658 archive entries in both, zero entries differing in content, and no entry present in one and absent from the other.

Method: cloned the repository at tag v2.0.0 with a clean working tree, ran the build below, and compared the result against the asset attached to the GitHub release. The comparison was done both on the whole-file SHA-256 and entry-by-entry across the ZIP contents.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/bitfinitechain/bitfinite-wallet
cd bitfinite-wallet
git checkout v2.0.0
VERSION=2.0.0 BUILD_NUM=8201 scripts/build-android-docker.sh release
sha256sum build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/app-arm64-v8a-release.apk
```

Requires Docker and roughly 20 minutes. No local Flutter, JDK, Rust or NDK installation is needed. The toolchain is inside the pinned image.

Why it reproduces: the entire build runs inside a Docker image pinned by digest (ghcr.io/bitfinitechain/bitfinitewallet-ci@sha256:193012d6983743632a3c5ccb87851bd192ab8921bed45414453afaaed3bc5f4f), so the host's Flutter, JDK, Rust and NDK versions do not affect the output. Dependencies are locked by pubspec.lock, including git dependencies pinned to commits.

BUILD_NUM is required, not optional. It sets versionCode inside the APK (arm64-v8a adds a +2000 ABI offset, giving 10201). Building without it produces a different binary for a reason unrelated to the source. The value for each release is recorded in doc/reproducible-builds.md.

Signing: APKs are signed with the project's release key using the v2 and v3 Android signature schemes. The signing block cannot be reproduced without that key; if you build unsigned, compare archive entries rather than the whole-file hash.

Known limitation: releases are currently built by a maintainer rather than by CI, because the repository has no signing secrets configured. The build is deterministic and pinned, but it does not yet run on a clean runner."}

{"description":"nunchuk-linux-v2.6.4.zip","content":"Update for **v2.6.4** (tag `2.6.4`, commit `27da37327db8aa59a87edce72546902c8343b25d`).

Unchanged from v2.6.2 and v2.6.3. The rebuild using `reproducible-builds/build_linux.sh` completes, and the extracted-SquashFS comparison against the published AppImage produces the same 85-entry pattern:

- 6 files differ — `bin/nunchuk-qt`, `bin/hwi`, `libcrypto.so`, `libcrypto.so.1.1`, `libolm.so.3`, `libqt5keychain.so.1`
- 3 libraries only in the published AppImage — `libcrypto.so.3`, `libssl.so.3`, `libpq.so.5`
- 76 libraries only in the rebuild (the `ldd` closure copied by `package_linux.sh`)

| Artifact | SHA-256 |
| --- | --- |
| `nunchuk-linux-v2.6.4.zip` | `5d7b4c36870df000c5501bbf532daf4e2bdd9f66bbd365b8edd8d1aa49b0ae26` |
| AppImage inside it (181,107,192 bytes) | `87ebfd10da31850442013bc918ca6532c33bc4c9cbf38a361e15bed406b0b195` |
| Our rebuilt AppImage (184,531,448 bytes) | `1113f30bc3988a8a2250c7c2bfcf1b17deb496a660a6db6a1a53249e437a62b6` |

Two things did improve on our side this time, both worth noting because they remove doubt about the inputs rather than the result:

- The ZIP hash matches your `SHA256SUMS`, and we verified `SHA256SUMS.asc` against release key `8C8ECD3F660CA53CD878792A6E38A462ED2EF525` — good signature. So we are comparing against the file you signed, not just the file we downloaded.
- We did not repeat the pipeline forensics for this release. The difference signature is identical to v2.6.2, so we are treating it as the same unchanged issue.

The five questions from the July 16 comment are still open. The two that would unblock us are unchanged:

1. Which workflow or job actually produces the release `nunchuk-linux-v*.zip`?
2. Can future Linux releases publish the AppImage built by `reproducible_linux.yml`, so the released file and the verifiable one are the same file?

One new question, on the compile-time OAuth values (`OAUTH_CLIENT_ID`, `OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`, `OAUTH_REDIRECT_URI`) that `reproducible_linux.yml` passes from repository secrets:

3. Can these be published, or a dummy set documented for verifiers? An outside rebuild has no access to them, so `bin/nunchuk-qt` cannot be byte-matched from public inputs alone. If the released builds are in fact produced with those secrets empty, saying so would also settle it — we cannot tell from the repository which is the case."}

## How Firmware Verification Works for Keystone3 Pro

Keystone3 Pro firmware is signed before release, so a naive comparison of official vs. independently built binaries will always differ. The repository ships a `firmware-checker` (`fmc`) Rust tool that extracts the unsigned payload checksum from a signed binary. The build process: clone the repo at the version tag, initialize submodules, build inside a containerized Ubuntu 20.04 environment with the exact Rust toolchain pinned in `rust-toolchain` and the same ARM `gcc-arm-none-eabi-9-2019-q4` cross-compiler used upstream, then run `build.py -e production` (no type flag for multicoin, the default). The resulting `mh1903.bin` is hashed and compared against the official binary's unsigned checksum (extracted via `fmc --source keystone3.bin`).

- Build container: Ubuntu 20.04 with Rust nightly (toolchain pinned via repo's `rust-toolchain` file) and ARM `gcc-arm-none-eabi-9-2019-q4-major` cross-compiler

## What This Means

- ✅ Built firmware matches the official firmware exactly, aside from the signature
- ✅ The production signature can't match since only Foundation Devices holds the release signing key
- ✅ Anyone can independently verify the build using the public repository and Foundation's own Nix recipe
- ✅ The code running on the device corresponds to the published source

## Build Environment

- Base image: `docker.io/nixos/nix:2.31.5`
- Toolchain: Foundation's own flake-pinned Rust toolchain (`rust-keyos`, via `flake.lock`), entered with `nix develop .#build`
- Build command: `scripts/generate-cosign2-dev-key.sh && cargo xtask build-all --production-bootloader --production-firmware` (Foundation's own `REPRODUCIBILITY.md` recipe, run verbatim)
- Hash extraction: `cargo xtask print-hashes` (Foundation's own tool; strips the 2048-byte cosign2 header before hashing, matching `xtask/src/bootimage.rs`)

---

## Scope and caveats

- **Bootloader (`boot.bin`) is excluded.** It's encrypted with a secret `EXTRA_ENTROPY` value held only by Foundation Devices and cannot be reproduced or verified by third parties. Foundation acknowledges this in `REPRODUCIBILITY.md` and states they are investigating ways to make it verifiable in the future.
- **Scope is the KeyOS image only.** Separate BLE and secure-element firmware were not tested.
- This review covers the `coresystemrecovery` type (`app.bin`) only, consistent with the v1.2.2 and v1.3.0 reviews — the `recovery` type (`recovery.bin`) has not yet been verified for any version.

---

## About Passport Prime / KeyOS

KeyOS is Foundation Devices' open-source (GPL-3.0-or-later), Xous-based operating system for the Passport Prime hardware wallet, running on a Microchip SAMA5D27 (ARM Cortex-A5). On this device, the OS *is* the firmware.

---

KeyOS v1.3.1 (coresystemrecovery) passes reproducible build verification using Foundation's own documented Nix recipe. Users of Passport Prime can have high confidence that the app image running on their device corresponds to the published, auditable source."}

The first attempt at this version failed with `ftbfs`:


doesn't apply to this chip.

invocations in `trezor_safe3_build.sh`, excluding `secmon`. Verified via the Makefile
that `build_secmon` has no dependents and no dependencies — it's fully independent from
`build_boardloader`/`build_bootloader`/`build_firmware` — so excluding it has no effect
on the artifacts being compared. This is a one-line script fix; no upstream source was
patched.

## What Went Wrong Before

`firmware.keepkey.bin` starts with a 256-byte header (magic `KPKY`, code length, three signature-index bytes, flags, and three 64-byte signature slots — see `tools/firmware/header.s`). A freshly built binary leaves that header zero-filled; the official release has it filled in with real signature data. By construction, the two full-file hashes can never match, signed or not — only the payload after byte 256 is meaningful for reproducibility.

Our script correctly stripped the header from the *official* binary (`73a880...`) but compared it against the *built* binary's **full, unstripped** hash (`7aa7ec...`) — a header-stripped hash can never equal an unstripped one, regardless of whether the underlying build is correct. That produced a false `not_reproducible` verdict on a build that was actually byte-for-byte correct.

The fix: strip the same 256 bytes from **both** sides before hashing. `keepkey_build.sh` has been corrected accordingly.

device-verifiable payload hash (`73a880...`), as documented in the release's HASHES.txt.

KeepKey v7.14.1 does not pass reproducible build verification. The firmware built from
commit `5482e7366a36e81336074f53a9defb6cff45ed72` via the official `release.sh` Docker

Cypherock X1 is an open-source hardware wallet that distributes key material across
four NFC smart cards (CyCards) using Shamir Secret Sharing. The device itself never
holds a complete private key; signing requires tapping at least one CyCard. The firmware
runs on an ARM Cortex-M4 and is built using CMake + Ninja via Cypherock's official
containerised toolchain.

Lilygo T-Display (ESP32) development board. It supports BIP39 seed management,
PSBT signing, xpub export, and QR code display. An air-gapped SD card mode is
available, though the primary interface is WebSerial over USB.

The project is in BETA and its own README advises testnet-only use or "an amount
of funds you are willing to lose."

## Notes

The project has no CI/CD pipeline, no Dockerfile, and no documented tool versions.
The official prebuilt binaries are committed directly into the repository under
`installer/firmware/esp32/v{VERSION}/` rather than being produced by any recorded
build process. This makes reproducibility very difficult to achieve in practice.

Arduino/ESP32 builds are non-deterministic by default: the toolchain embeds
compilation timestamps and other variable metadata into the output binary.
Reproducing a byte-identical binary would require knowing the exact Arduino IDE
version, ESP32 core version, and host environment used by the original developer —
none of which are documented.

The firmware compiled cleanly (501 KB, 38% of available flash) using ESP32 core
2.0.17, which is required for compatibility with the bundled TFT_eSPI v2.2.20
library. The ESP32 core 3.x series removed the direct GPIO register access API
that this library version relies on."}

{"description":"Binary obtained from the manufacturer's website","content":"# Foundation Devices KeyOS v1.2.0 (Passport Prime) — Recovery Verification Review

## Overview

KeyOS is the firmware for the Passport Prime hardware wallet by Foundation Devices.
It runs on a SAMA5D27 ARM Cortex-A5 processor using the xous microkernel, written
entirely in Rust.

This review covers the `recovery.bin` image — the recovery OS firmware — distributed as
`KeyOS-v1.2.0-Recovery.bin` in the GitHub release.

Repository: https://github.com/Foundation-Devices/KeyOS

---

## What Can Be Verified

Foundation's own REPRODUCIBILITY.md is explicit about what can and cannot be verified:

| Binary         | Verifiable | Reason                                         |
|----------------|------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `recovery.bin` | Yes        | SHA256 compared after stripping cosign2 header |
| `boot.bin`     | **No**     | Encrypted with a secret key for secure boot    |

**The bootloader (`boot.bin`) is not reproducible.** It is encrypted with a secret
`EXTRA_ENTROPY` value held only by Foundation Devices. No third party can reproduce
or verify it. Foundation acknowledges this in their documentation and states they are
investigating ways to make it verifiable in the future.

This is a critical limitation. The bootloader is the root of trust on the device — it
runs before any user-verifiable code and is responsible for validating the firmware
signature. An unverifiable bootloader can silently bypass all firmware integrity checks,
defeating the purpose of reproducible firmware above it.

---

## Build Details

| Field         | Value                                                                 |
|---------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Repository    | https://github.com/Foundation-Devices/KeyOS                           |
| Version       | 1.2.0                                                                 |
| Tag           | `v1.2.0`                                                              |
| Artifact      | `recovery.bin` → released as `KeyOS-v1.2.0-Recovery.bin`             |
| Target CPU    | SAMA5D27 (ARM Cortex-A5), `armv7a-unknown-xous-elf`                   |
| Language      | Rust (nightly-2025-09-11)                                             |
| Build command | `cargo xtask build-all --production-bootloader --production-firmware` |
| Official env  | Nix flake (aarch64 recommended for perfect reproducibility)           |
| Signing       | cosign2 (secp256k1); first 2048 bytes stripped before comparison      |
| Dependencies  | All pinned via `Cargo.lock` and `rust-toolchain.toml`                 |

---

## Verification Results

> Build in progress. Hashes will be updated once a successful build completes.

**Verdict: TBD**

| File            | SHA256 |
|-----------------|--------|
| `recovery.bin` (official, signed)   | TBD |
| `recovery.bin` (official, stripped) | TBD |
| `recovery.bin` (built)              | TBD |

Hash comparison method:

```bash
tail -c +2049 KeyOS-v1.2.0-Recovery.bin | sha256sum
```

---

## Notes

- Foundation's REPRODUCIBILITY.md explicitly states aarch64 is required for perfect
  reproducibility. This build ran on x86_64, which may cause a mismatch — Rust's
  codegen can produce different output across architectures
- The custom Rust target `armv7a-unknown-xous-elf` is distributed by Foundation from
  their own GitHub releases, not from official Rust toolchain infrastructure
- The [KeyOS-Releases](https://github.com/Foundation-Devices/KeyOS-Releases) repository
  referenced in Foundation's reproducibility documentation only contains v1.0.0 at the
  time of writing; v1.2.0 comparison binaries are only available via GitHub release assets"}

## Verification Results

```text
Built firmware hash:    be035a4e23a5c208f85d57b89065521facaf209d032fa847fe2eaec200f350c2
Released firmware hash: c82a6037f2c2b541c22154731a1f00662dcbdf24fbb5af57127c47e63b5616f1
```

## Verdict: NOT REPRODUCIBLE ✗

Cypherock X1 v0.6.3330 does not pass strict byte-for-byte reproducible build verification. The locally built firmware hash differs from the officially released firmware.

## Technical Details

| Field      | Value                                                 |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| Firmware   | Cypherock X1                                          |
| Version    | `0.6.3330`                                            |
| Verdict    | `not_reproducible`                                    |
| Repository | `https://github.com/Cypherock/x1_wallet_firmware.git` |
| Tag        | `v0.6.3330`                                           |
| Commit     | `65d5104679c0223ec520018630381bba318b223a`            |

## Hashes

| Artifact          | SHA256                                                             |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Built firmware    | `be035a4e23a5c208f85d57b89065521facaf209d032fa847fe2eaec200f350c2` |
| Released firmware | `c82a6037f2c2b541c22154731a1f00662dcbdf24fbb5af57127c47e63b5616f1` |

## Root Cause Analysis

Although the firmware fails strict reproducibility checks, the mismatch appears to come from version-string metadata rather than differences in compiled code.

The binaries differ by only 7 bytes located at offset `0xa1a8c`. The released firmware embeds the string:

```text
v0.6.3330
```

while the locally reproduced build embeds:

```text
0.6.3330
```

The only distinction is the missing `v` prefix. File sizes remain identical, and the compiled firmware payload is otherwise byte-for-byte equivalent.

## Why This Happens

The firmware derives its embedded version string dynamically during build time using:

```text
git describe --exact-match --tags
```

via:

```text
utilities/cmake/version.cmake
```

At the time the official release was built, the commit only carried the tag:

```text
v0.6.3330
```

As a result, the official firmware embedded the prefixed version string.

Later, an additional tag without the prefix:

```text
0.6.3330
```

was added to the exact same commit. Git now resolves the non-prefixed tag first, causing current source builds to embed the alternate version string.

This creates a reproducibility mismatch even though the underlying compiled firmware code remains unchanged.

## Historical Context

Earlier Cypherock X1 releases such as:

* `v0.6.3328`
* `v0.6.3329`

contain only a single canonical `v`-prefixed tag and reproduce correctly without issue.

Version `0.6.3330` appears to be the first release where both prefixed and non-prefixed tags coexist on the same commit.

## Suggested Fix

Cypherock could resolve this issue in either of two ways:

1. Remove the duplicate non-prefixed tag:

   ```text
   0.6.3330
   ```

2. Make the build system explicitly prefer canonical release tags by changing:

   ```text
   git describe --exact-match --tags
   ```

   to:

   ```text
   git describe --exact-match --tags --match 'v*'
   ```

This would ensure deterministic version selection even if multiple tags exist on the same commit.

## Conclusion

Cypherock X1 v0.6.3330 fails strict byte-for-byte reproducible build verification due to a post-release tagging inconsistency affecting the embedded version string. The observed mismatch does not appear to impact the compiled firmware logic or security-relevant code, which remains otherwise identical to the official release."}

ADAMANT Messenger version 4.10.6 verification failed due to build errors. The containerized build could not complete.

```
Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find package 'dotenv' 
imported from /app/scripts/capacitor/build-android.mjs
```

The build script attempts to import `dotenv`, but Node.js cannot locate it despite being installed. This indicates:
- The package may need to be in `devDependencies` instead
- ESM module resolution issues in Node.js 20
- Missing entry in package.json

### Node.js Version Mismatch

The Dockerfile uses Node.js 20, but Klayr packages require Node.js 18:
```
required: { node: '>=18.12.0 <=18' }
```

**Repository**: https://github.com/lnflash/flash-mobile  
**Type**: React Native Bitcoin wallet with Breez SDK  

## Build Results

**Environment**: Docker (Ubuntu 22.04, Android SDK 33, Node.js 18)

### What Worked ✅
- Dependencies installed successfully (`yarn install`)
- 68+ React Native modules compiled including Breez SDK, Firebase modules, crypto libraries
- All native Android code and NDK components processed correctly

### Build Failure ❌
```
File google-services.json is missing. The Google Services Plugin cannot function without it.
```

## Repository Analysis

**Provides**:
- Complete source code
- Standard build instructions (`yarn install` → `yarn android`)

**Missing**:
- `google-services.json` (Firebase configuration file)
- No documentation on obtaining this file
- No alternative build without Firebase
- No mock/sample configuration files

## Verdict: FTBFS (Fails To Build From Source)

**Reason**: Repository requires external Firebase configuration file not provided or documented. Build process expects `google-services.json` but gives no instructions for creating/obtaining it.

**Classification**: Configuration dependency failure - 100% reproducible failure for any developer without Firebase setup.

**Fix Required**: Repository maintainers need to provide either:
- Sample `google-services.json` file for building
- Instructions for Firebase setup  
- Firebase-free build configuration
- Clear documentation of external requirements

The codebase quality is high and all complex native integrations work correctly, but the build configuration is incomplete for independent compilation."}

Samourai has cost me many many hours due to their strong social media presence and constant ad hominem attacks. They blamed me for not being able to compile or reproduce their product instead of helping me to compile it. Given I compile wallets all the time as can be found on walletscrutiny, I doubt I lack the expertise to compile wallets but even if I did, why not show me? Not one developer other than their team themselves disagreed with my technical assessments of their product. Apart from proven scams, this is the product I trust least in the whole space.

But it's not only me. To [quote Bitcoin Core developer and absolute genius Gregory Maxwell](https://www.reddit.com/r/Bitcoin/comments/9r9344/slp29_samourai_wallet_bitcoin_privacy_software/e8fm1v8/):

> I have seen far too much outright dishonest and extremely incompetent behaviour from Samourai to ever trust it myself.
> Samourai has very poor privacy while bragging about having good privacy: It sends your addresses all back to their server. Their "trusted node" mode doesn't change this, it just exposes your Bitcoin node to attacks completely needlessly. (Needlessly because they only use it to relay transactions, which they could do via the public P2P ports of any node, and because since they've already sent your addresses back to their server sending your transactions via something else doesn't increase your privacy.)
> If you want strong privacy then as a start you need to run a full node (and use either Bitcoin Core wallet, or run your own electrum server), preferably via tor.
> I don't doubt that they want and intend to eventually have good privacy but it seems that they're just unable to stop lying about it, even after previously being caught.

You can find many more very competent people complaining about Samourai's dishonesity and aggressive behavior or outright incompetence if not malice [here](https://nopara73.medium.com/samouraileaks-samouraidevs-sockpuppet-exposed-7ce654b92c0b), [here](https://nopara73.medium.com/samouraileaks-part-2-harassment-of-bitcoin-developers-fae3019abd2f), [here](https://nopara73.medium.com/samouraileaks-part-3-is-random-org-random-enough-35704796ae93), and [here](https://github.com/nopara73/ScamouraiWallet/). Stay away from Scamourai!

Opinion about Bitcoin Wallet (android)
<!--HEADER END-->
The Schildbach Bitcoin Wallet was the very first open source Bitcoin wallet and as it was open source from the start, many built on its source code, including most of the first alt-coin wallets. As a result, of all the Android wallets it is certainly the one with most eyes on it but it's also a bit dated. Its developers keep contributing and new versions are released every other week.

Its very limited feature set also means that the code base is rather limited, resulting in a small attack surface.
Its at times unconventional ways of doing things might confuse users coming from other wallets. For example, when requesting a payment, the app only shows a QR-Code and no receive address. The backup is not a 12 words mnemonic but an encrypted file that you have to remember the passphrase for. For me personally the least attractive about this product is that it connects to multiple Bitcoin full nodes and if that hasn't changed, it also connects to random ones. As chain analysis companies run such nodes in big numbers, these companies probably learn your IP address and all your Bitcoin addresses with every transaction you make.

In summary, this wallet is great to not lose your coins to random backdoors or bugs but not so great for your privacy or convenience.
